w: Only Yellowstone came before it: signed into law by Ulysses S. Grant in 1875, Mackinac National Park covered 1,044 acres and was run by the Fort Mackinac garrison, whose soldiers served as caretakers since Congress gave the park no operating budget of its own. It survived instead on leased building lots. Twenty years later, in 1895, Michigan's governor asked for it back, and it became the state's first state park.
s: America's second national park, run by an army fort
_facts: second US national park after Yellowstone, established 1875
1,044 acres, run by the Fort Mackinac garrison with no federal funding
transferred to state control in 1895

w: Called Nissawinagong by Native Americans, this 378-acre island is nominally part of the City of Mackinac Island but is actually overseen by the U.S. Forest Service as a wilderness area within Hiawatha National Forest. No one lives here. An estimated 900,000 ferry passengers a year pass close by on their way to Mackinac Island, whose harbor the uninhabited island helps shelter.
s: Uninhabited island 900,000 ferry riders pass yearly
_facts: 378-acre uninhabited island, Round Island Wilderness Area within Hiawatha National Forest
overseen by the US Forest Service though nominally part of Mackinac Island
roughly 900,000 tourists a year pass it by ferry

w: M-185, the road ringing this park, is the only state highway in Michigan with no cars allowed, matching the island-wide ban. The park covers 1,800 acres, roughly 80 percent of Mackinac Island, and became Michigan's first state park in 1895 when it took over from the defunct Mackinac National Park. It welcomed its 20-millionth visitor on July 15, 2009.
s: Michigan's first state park, ringed by a car-free road
_facts: 1,800 acres, about 80% of Mackinac Island
M-185 circles it as Michigan's only motorless state highway
became Michigan's first state park in 1895; 20-millionth visitor in 2009

w: Alexis de Tocqueville stopped here in August 1831 and described a 'Giant's Arch of extraordinary shape.' The 146-foot limestone arch formed during a post-glacial high-water period in Lake Huron, a rare survival since limestone breccia doesn't usually hold together into natural bridges. Native Americans regarded it as a place of numinous power, and its presence helped justify creating Mackinac National Park in 1875.
s: A 146-foot limestone arch de Tocqueville admired
_facts: natural limestone arch, 146 ft above Lake Huron
formed during the post-glacial Nipissing high-water period
described by Alexis de Tocqueville in 1831; helped justify Mackinac National Park in 1875

w: The British built this fort during the Revolutionary War to control the Straits of Mackinac and the fur trade running through them, then refused to hand it over for thirteen years after the war ended. It changed hands again during two battles in the War of 1812. The U.S. Army held it for most of the 19th century until it closed in 1895; it now runs as a museum within Mackinac Island State Park.
s: British-built fort held 13 years past war's end
_facts: built by the British during the Revolutionary War to control the Straits and fur trade
scene of two battles in the War of 1812
US Army outpost until 1895, now a museum

w: Its porch is advertised as the longest in the world, built up in stages as a coastal resort through the late 19th century. Five U.S. presidents have stayed here, along with Thomas Edison and Mark Twain. It has kept its old-money profile ever since as a member of Historic Hotels of America, a National Trust for Historic Preservation program recognizing hotels of enduring historic character.
s: World's longest porch, hosted five presidents and Twain
_facts: advertises the world's largest porch
guests have included five US presidents, Thomas Edison, and Mark Twain
member of Historic Hotels of America

w: Built by the British in 1814 to threaten Fort Mackinac from the island's highest point, this earthen redoubt started life as Fort George. When Americans reclaimed the island under the Treaty of Ghent in 1815, they renamed it for Major Andrew Holmes, killed that same year in the Battle of Mackinac Island. The Army abandoned it soon after; the WPA rebuilt it from an 1817 survey in 1936, though only the earthworks remain today.
s: Britain's redoubt, renamed for a fallen American major
_facts: built by the British in 1814 as Fort George, on the island's highest point
renamed Fort Holmes in 1815 for Major Andrew Holmes
rebuilt by the WPA from an 1817 survey in 1936

w: Housed in the island's historic Indian Dormitory building, the collection here runs from 19th-century paintings and maps to Native American beadwork and contemporary photography by island-based artists. It is one of several museums the Mackinac Island State Park Commission operates alongside the forts, Arch Rock, and the rest of the park's historic sites.
s: Island art housed in the historic Indian Dormitory
_facts: housed in the historic Indian Dormitory building
exhibits historic painting, maps, photographs, and Native American beaded garments
run by the Mackinac Island State Park Commission

w: Ferries bound for Mackinac Island pass this red-stone-and-wood lighthouse on Round Island's west shore, built because the island itself was judged a hazard to shipping in the Straits of Mackinac. Its stubby, old-fashioned-schoolhouse profile has made it one of the most recognizable landmarks on the upper Great Lakes.
s: A schoolhouse-shaped lighthouse guarding the straits
_facts: also called the Old Round Island Point Lighthouse
built to warn shipping away from Round Island in the Straits of Mackinac
red stone base and wood tower, likened to a schoolhouse

w: Built in 1829, this Congregational church is the oldest surviving church building in Michigan, predating the state's admission to the Union by eight years. It rose among an island population that was still largely French and Metis, whose own Sainte Anne parish already predated it, though Sainte Anne's current building dates only to 1874. Mission Church has been listed on the National Register since 1971.
s: Michigan's oldest surviving church, built in 1829
_facts: built 1829, oldest surviving church building in Michigan
Sainte Anne parish, serving the island's French/Metis population, predates it
listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1971
